sections.title: Dedication
sections.html:
Dedication

For every home baker who has ever looked through the glass of a French bakery and thought, “I wish I could make that.”

You can.

This book is for beginners willing to get flour on the counter, butter on their hands, and occasionally produce something that looks nothing like the photograph. It is for people willing to try again.

Somewhere between the first imperfect loaf and the first beautiful croissant, something changes: you stop simply following recipes and begin becoming a baker.

sections.title: Preface
sections.html:
Preface

Why Twenty-Eight Days?

French baking can look intimidating because the finished product hides the process. You see the crisp baguette, the layered croissant, the glossy éclair, or the perfect fruit tart. You do not see the resting, folding, waiting, temperature adjustments, imperfect batches, and repetition behind it.

This book is built around a sequence rather than a giant collection of unrelated recipes. You begin with flour, water, salt, yeast, and time. You learn to recognize fermentation and gluten development before you are asked to laminate butter into croissant dough. Then you move into enriched dough, tart pastry, custards, choux, lamination, and finally production.

Twenty-eight days cannot replace years of professional training, but four focused weeks can create a genuine foundation. The goal is not to compete with a Paris pâtissier. The goal is to become dramatically better than you were on Day One.

sections.title: Author Introduction
sections.html:
Author Introduction

I wrote French Baking in 28 Days around one simple idea: difficult skills become learnable when they are broken into achievable steps.

A recipe tells you what to do. A teacher also tells you what you should see, feel, smell, and notice while you are doing it. That is the approach throughout this program.

Some recipes return later in the book on purpose. Your second baguette teaches lessons your first could not. Your third croissant batch reveals details that were invisible in your first. Repetition is not wasted time; it is how information becomes skill.

Tie your apron, take out your measuring tools, and begin. Day One exists because you are not ready yet. That is the point.

sections.title: How to Use This Book
sections.html:
How to Use This Book

Follow the days in order. Each week is designed to build on the last. Keep a baker’s notebook and record kitchen temperature, fermentation time, proofing time, what worked, what failed, and what you will change next time.

Remember the central rule of the program:

The clock tells you when to look. The dough tells you when it is ready.

sections.title: Baking Without a Scale
sections.html:
Baking Without a Scale

You can complete this entire 28-day program using standard U.S. measuring cups and spoons. The gram measurements remain in every recipe because they are the most precise method for French baking, but the household measurements beside them are designed for readers who do not own a scale.

How to Measure Flour

Do not dip the measuring cup directly into the flour bag. First loosen the flour with a spoon. Spoon flour lightly into the measuring cup without packing it down, then sweep the excess level with the straight edge of a knife. This “spoon-and-level” method is the basis for the cup conversions in this book.

Liquids

Use a clear liquid measuring cup on a level surface. Bend down and read the measurement at eye level. For tablespoons and teaspoons, fill the spoon to the rim without overflowing.

Butter

U.S. butter wrappers are especially convenient: 1 stick = 1/2 cup = 8 tablespoons = about 113 g. Two sticks equal about 1 cup or 227 g.

Yeast, Salt, and Tiny Quantities

Use measuring spoons for yeast and salt and level them carefully. A standard packet of instant or active dry yeast contains about 2 1/4 teaspoons (7 g). For the tiny amount of yeast used in the Day 25 poolish, use only a very small pinch; this quantity is intentionally approximate without a precision scale.

A Note About Cups

Volume measurements are practical, but flour can settle and measuring cups differ slightly. If a dough seems unusually dry, do not immediately add all the remaining flour or liquid. Use the visual and tactile cues in each lesson. For croissants and other advanced pastries, grams remain the preferred method whenever a scale is available.

Essential Equipment

Digital kitchen scale

Mixing bowls

Bench scraper and bowl scraper

Whisk and silicone spatula

Rolling pin

Pastry brush

Baking sheets and parchment

Cooling rack

Instant-read thermometer

Fine-mesh sieve

Bread lame or very sharp blade

Loaf pan and tart pan

Saucepan

Piping bags and round/star tips

Clean kitchen towels

Optional but helpful: stand mixer, baking stone/steel, couche, madeleine pan, oven thermometer

Master Ingredients

All recipes now include both gram weights and practical U.S. cup/spoon equivalents.

Bread flour and all-purpose flour

Almond flour

Instant yeast

Fine salt

Granulated and confectioners’ sugar

Unsalted butter

Whole milk and heavy cream

Large eggs

Cornstarch

Vanilla

Dark chocolate and chocolate batons

Fresh seasonal fruit and apples

Apricot preserves

Sliced almonds and optional praline paste

Temperature Reference

300°F = 150°C | 325°F = 165°C | 350°F = 175°C | 375°F = 190°C | 400°F = 205°C | 425°F = 220°C | 450°F = 230°C | 475°F = 245°C

Dough changes from rough and shaggy to elastic through hydration, rest, and folding.

sections.title: DAY 1
sections.html:
DAY 1

Think Like a Baker

Yield: 1 practice dough

Active time: 20 min

Total time: About 2 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind think like a baker through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

250 g (about 2 cups) bread flour

165 g (about 2/3 cup + 2 tsp) lukewarm water

5 g (about 3/4 tsp) fine salt

2 g (about 2/3 tsp) instant yeast

Step by Step

1. Weigh every ingredient in grams.

2. Mix flour and yeast, add water, then salt. Stop when no dry flour remains.

3. Rest 20 minutes.

4. Perform three sets of stretch-and-folds, 20 minutes apart.

5. Place dough in a container, mark its height, and observe fermentation.

What You Should See and Feel

At first the dough looks rough and feels sticky. After resting and folding it becomes smoother, stronger, and more elastic. A small piece should eventually stretch thinner before tearing.

Baker's Note

Do not add flour simply because the dough feels sticky. Today is about learning hydration, gluten, and fermentation—not producing a perfect loaf.

From shaggy dough to stronger, more elastic dough.

DAY 2

Your First French Loaf

Yield: 1 medium boule

Active time: 35–45 min

Total time: 3–4 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind your first french loaf through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

400 g (about 3 1/3 cups) bread flour

280 g (about 1 cup + 3 tbsp) water

8 g (about 1 1/3 tsp) fine salt

4 g (about 1 1/4 tsp) instant yeast

Step by Step

1. Mix flour with 260 g water and rest 20 minutes.

2. Add yeast, salt, and remaining water.

3. Perform three sets of folds during early bulk fermentation.

4. Ferment until visibly expanded and airy.

5. Preshape into a round; rest 15–20 minutes.

6. Final-shape into a boule and proof until puffy.

7. Score and bake at 450°F / 230°C, ideally with steam or in a covered vessel; uncover to finish deeply browned.

8. Cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

What You Should See and Feel

The dough should become lighter and more aerated as fermentation progresses. Properly proofed dough slowly springs back after a gentle press.

Baker's Note

Dense crumb usually points to underproofing, weak gluten, or overly aggressive shaping. Pale bread usually needs more heat or time.

DAY 3

The French Baguette

Photorealistic reference: shaping, scoring, and the finished French baguette.

Yield: 3 baguettes

Active time: 45 min

Total time: About 4 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind the french baguette through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

500 g (about 4 1/4 cups) bread flour

340 g (about 1 1/3 cups + 1 1/2 tbsp) water

10 g fine salt

4 g (about 1 1/4 tsp) instant yeast

Step by Step

1. Mix flour with 320 g water; rest 20–30 minutes.

2. Add yeast, salt, and remaining water.

3. Bulk ferment about 2 hours with two or three folds early in the process.

4. Divide into three equal pieces and preshape short cylinders.

5. Rest 20 minutes.

6. Shape gently into even baguettes.

7. Proof seam-side up in a floured couche or towel.

8. Score with overlapping cuts running mostly along the loaf.

9. Bake with steam at 450–475°F / 230–245°C until richly browned.

What You Should See and Feel

The dough should lengthen without tearing. If it fights you, rest it. The finished baguette should feel light, have a crisp crust, opened scores, and an aerated crumb.

Baker's Note

Do not saw at the dough when scoring. Use a confident, quick motion with a sharp blade.

Baguette scoring should overlap and travel mostly along the loaf.

DAY 4

The Better Baguette

Yield: 3 baguettes

Active time: 45 min

Total time: About 4 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind the better baguette through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

Repeat Day 3 formula

Step by Step

1. Identify yesterday’s biggest weakness.

2. Choose one likely cause.

3. Repeat the baguette formula while changing only one major variable.

4. Photograph and compare the results.

What You Should See and Feel

Look for a measurable improvement in shape, scoring, color, crust, or crumb.

Baker's Note

Changing five things at once teaches you very little. Controlled repetition is how bakers learn.

DAY 5

Brioche

Yield: 1 large loaf

Active time: 45–60 min

Total time: 6 hr to overnight

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind brioche through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

500 g (about 4 1/4 cups) bread flour

60 g (about 1/4 cup + 1 tbsp) sugar

10 g (about 1 2/3 tsp) salt

7 g (about 2 1/4 tsp / 1 packet) instant yeast

250 g eggs (about 5 large eggs)

60 g (1/4 cup) whole milk

225 g (1 cup / 2 sticks) unsalted butter, soft but not greasy

Step by Step

1. Combine flour, sugar, and yeast; add eggs and milk.

2. Develop gluten before adding most of the butter.

3. Add salt, then incorporate butter gradually.

4. Continue mixing until smooth, glossy, and elastic.

5. Begin fermentation at room temperature, then refrigerate several hours or overnight.

6. Shape chilled dough into equal balls and place in a greased loaf pan.

7. Proof until light and expanded.

8. Egg-wash and bake at 350°F / 175°C until deeply burnished and cooked through.

What You Should See and Feel

Finished brioche dough is supple, glossy, and elastic rather than greasy batter. The baked crumb should pull into tender strands.

Baker's Note

If butter refuses to incorporate, it may be too cold or the dough may need more gluten development.

DAY 6

Beautiful Brioche

Yield: 1 braid plus rolls

Active time: 30–40 min

Total time: Several hours

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind beautiful brioche through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

1 batch Day 5 brioche dough

1 egg + 1 tbsp milk for egg wash

Step by Step

1. Divide chilled dough accurately by weight.

2. Shape three ropes and braid one portion without pulling tightly.

3. Shape remaining dough into smooth rolls by creating surface tension against the counter.

4. Proof until expanded and delicate.

5. Egg-wash gently and bake at 350°F / 175°C until deeply golden.

What You Should See and Feel

Uniform pieces should proof and bake at similar rates. Smooth, tight surfaces produce cleaner shapes.

Baker's Note

Do not crush fully proofed brioche with heavy egg washing.

DAY 8

Pâte Sucrée

Yield: 1 9-inch / 23-cm tart shell

Active time: 25 min

Total time: About 2 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind pâte sucrée through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

250 g (about 2 cups) all-purpose flour

125 g (about 1/2 cup + 1 tbsp) unsalted butter, softened

90 g (about 3/4 cup) confectioners’ sugar

30 g (about 1/4 cup) almond flour

1 large egg

2 g (about 1/3 tsp) salt

1 tsp vanilla

Step by Step

1. Mix butter and confectioners’ sugar until smooth.

2. Add almond flour, salt, egg, and vanilla.

3. Add flour and stop as soon as cohesive.

4. Flatten, wrap, and chill at least 1 hour.

5. Roll about 3 mm thick and fit into tart pan without stretching.

6. Chill again, then blind-bake at 350°F / 175°C until set; remove weights and finish lightly golden.

What You Should See and Feel

The dough should be cohesive but not elastic like bread dough. A baked shell should hold sharp edges and have a dry base.

Baker's Note

Shrinkage usually means overworking, stretching, or insufficient chilling.

DAY 9

Crème Pâtissière

Photorealistic reference: pastry cream from tempering through the finished silky texture.

Yield: About 600 g

Active time: 20 min

Total time: 2+ hr including chilling

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind crème pâtissière through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

500 g (about 2 cups + 2 tbsp) whole milk

100 g (1/2 cup) sugar, divided

4 large egg yolks

40 g (about 5 tbsp) cornstarch

30 g (2 tbsp) unsalted butter

2 tsp vanilla

Step by Step

1. Heat milk with half the sugar until steaming.

2. Whisk yolks with remaining sugar and cornstarch.

3. Temper with hot milk gradually while whisking.

4. Return to saucepan and cook over medium heat, whisking constantly, until thick and bubbling.

5. Cook briefly after thickening, remove from heat, and add butter and vanilla.

6. Spread in a shallow container, cover surface directly, and refrigerate promptly.

What You Should See and Feel

Finished pastry cream is smooth, glossy, and thick enough to hold a soft ridge.

Baker's Note

If thin, it may not have cooked sufficiently after thickening. If lumpy, whisk vigorously and pass through a fine sieve while warm.

Temper yolks by adding hot milk gradually while whisking.

DAY 10

Tarte aux Fruits

Yield: 1 9-inch tart

Active time: 30 min assembly

Total time: About 3 hr with components

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind tarte aux fruits through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

1 baked pâte sucrée shell

About 500 g pastry cream

2–3 cups fresh seasonal fruit

Apricot preserves + water, optional

Step by Step

1. Cool the tart shell completely.

2. Whisk chilled pastry cream briefly until smooth.

3. Fill and level the shell.

4. Arrange fruit from the outer edge inward in deliberate patterns.

5. Optionally brush with a very thin strained apricot glaze.

6. Refrigerate until serving.

What You Should See and Feel

The tart should look intentional: crisp shell, level cream, fresh fruit, clean edges.

Baker's Note

Best assembled the day it will be served.

DAY 11

Madeleines

Yield: About 18

Active time: 25 min

Total time: About 2 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind madeleines through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

120 g (about 1/2 cup) unsalted butter

2 large eggs

100 g (1/2 cup) sugar

120 g (about 1 cup) all-purpose flour

4 g (1 tsp) baking powder

Pinch salt

Zest of 1 lemon

1 tsp vanilla

Step by Step

1. Brown the butter until nutty and golden; cool.

2. Whisk eggs and sugar until slightly lightened.

3. Add zest and vanilla.

4. Fold in flour, baking powder, and salt.

5. Fold in cooled brown butter.

6. Chill batter at least 1 hour.

7. Fill prepared molds about three-quarters full and bake at 375°F / 190°C for 9–12 minutes.

What You Should See and Feel

Look for golden edges, a springy center, and the characteristic hump.

Baker's Note

Brown butter can go from nutty to burned quickly. Remove it as soon as the milk solids turn golden.

DAY 12

Pâte à Choux

Yield: About 24 small puffs

Active time: 30 min

Total time: About 1½ hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind pâte à choux through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

125 g (1/2 cup) water

125 g (1/2 cup) whole milk

100 g (7 tbsp) unsalted butter

5 g (about 1 1/4 tsp) sugar

4 g (about 2/3 tsp) salt

150 g (about 1 1/4 cups) all-purpose flour

200–250 g beaten egg (about 4–5 large eggs), added gradually

Step by Step

1. Bring water, milk, butter, sugar, and salt to a boil.

2. Add flour all at once and stir vigorously.

3. Cook until a cohesive panade forms and a light film appears on the pan.

4. Cool slightly.

5. Add beaten egg gradually, checking consistency after each addition.

6. Pipe rounds.

7. Bake around 400°F / 205°C until expanded, then reduce toward 350°F / 175°C and continue until deeply golden and dry.

What You Should See and Feel

Correct choux falls slowly from the spatula and forms a smooth V. Baked shells should feel light and hollow.

Baker's Note

Do not blindly add all the egg. The correct amount depends on how much moisture was cooked out of the panade.

The choux V-test: batter falls slowly and forms a smooth V.

DAY 13

Éclairs au Chocolat

Yield: About 10 éclairs

Active time: 45 min

Total time: 3+ hr with chilling

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind éclairs au chocolat through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

1 batch pâte à choux

1 batch pastry cream

100 g (about 2/3 cup chopped) dark chocolate for filling

150 g (about 1 cup chopped) dark chocolate + 120 g (1/2 cup) heavy cream for ganache

Step by Step

1. Pipe 4–5 inch choux lines and bake until deeply golden and dry.

2. Stir 100 g chopped dark chocolate into warm pastry cream; chill.

3. Make small holes underneath cooled éclairs and pipe in filling.

4. Heat cream, pour over 150 g chocolate, rest 1 minute, then stir smooth.

5. Dip éclair tops in ganache and chill briefly to set.

What You Should See and Feel

A good éclair feels light before filling and noticeably heavier afterward. The glaze should be thin, glossy, and clean.

Baker's Note

Keep filled éclairs refrigerated and enjoy within about 24 hours for best texture.

Ingredients

Step by Step

2. Use resting and chilling periods to prepare other components.

3. Assemble the tart only when shell and cream are cold.

4. Fill and glaze éclairs after shells are fully cooled.

5. Photograph and evaluate tart dough, pastry cream, piping, choux, presentation, and organization.

You should begin recognizing which components can be prepared ahead and which are best finished near serving time.

Baker's Note

Professional-looking pastry depends as much on organization as on recipes.

DAY 15

Understanding Lamination

Yield: Technique day

Active time: 20 min

Total time: About 45 min

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind understanding lamination through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

100 g cool unsalted butter for practice

Step by Step

1. Place butter between parchment.

2. Tap and roll into an even rectangle.

3. Observe how butter behaves when too cold, properly pliable, and too warm.

4. Learn the vocabulary: détrempe, beurrage, lock-in, turn, proof.

What You Should See and Feel

Proper lamination butter bends without shattering and does not feel greasy.

Baker's Note

Your three enemies are excessive heat, excessive cold, and impatience.

Lamination creates alternating dough and butter layers.

DAY 16

Croissant Dough & Butter Block

Photorealistic reference: croissant dough, butter block, and laminated folds.

Yield: About 12 croissants

Active time: 45 min

Total time: Overnight recommended

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind croissant dough & butter block through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

500 g (about 4 1/4 cups) bread flour

60 g (about 1/4 cup + 1 tbsp) sugar

10 g (about 1 2/3 tsp) salt

10 g instant yeast

140 g (about 1/2 cup + 1 tbsp) cold whole milk

140 g (about 1/2 cup + 1 tbsp) cold water

40 g (about 3 tbsp) softened butter

280 g (about 1 1/4 cups / 2 1/2 sticks) unsalted butter for lamination

Step by Step

1. Mix dough ingredients and develop moderate gluten.

2. Shape into a neat rectangle, wrap, and chill thoroughly.

3. Place lamination butter between parchment.

4. Tap and roll butter into an even rectangle.

5. Chill until firm but pliable.

What You Should See and Feel

Dough and butter should have similar flexibility before lock-in.

Baker's Note

If the butter is rock hard while the dough is flexible, it can fracture; if greasy-soft, it can smear.

sections.title: DAY 16 COMPLETE ✓
sections.html:

DAY 17

Lock-In and Turns

Yield: Laminated dough

Active time: 35 min active

Total time: 2+ hr with rests

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind lock-in and turns through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

Chilled Day 16 dough

Prepared butter block

Step by Step

1. Roll dough large enough to enclose butter.

2. Lock in butter and seal without thick overlapping seams.

3. Roll lengthwise with even pressure.

4. Fold into thirds like a letter; brush away excess flour.

5. Chill about 30 minutes.

6. Rotate 90 degrees, roll, and fold again.

7. Repeat for a third single turn if using this method; chill at least 1 hour or overnight.

What You Should See and Feel

The dough should remain smooth, cool, and even. No butter should leak through the surface.

Baker's Note

If butter softens, stop and refrigerate. Twenty minutes of patience can save the batch.

Keep laminated layers even and cool during turns.

DAY 18

Your First Croissants

Photorealistic reference: cutting, shaping, proofing, and the honeycomb interior.

Yield: About 12

Active time: 35 min active

Total time: 3–4 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind your first croissants through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

1 batch laminated croissant dough

1 egg + 1 tbsp milk or water for egg wash

Step by Step

1. Roll dough to about 3–4 mm thick.

2. Trim edges and cut consistent long triangles.

3. Gently lengthen each triangle and roll from base to tip without crushing layers.

4. Place tip underneath.

5. Proof until clearly expanded and slightly jiggly when the tray moves.

6. Egg-wash gently.

7. Bake around 390–400°F / 200°C for roughly 18–24 minutes until richly golden.

8. Cool before cutting one open.

What You Should See and Feel

Properly proofed croissants look swollen and delicate. Inside, aim for defined layers and an open honeycomb rather than tight bread-like crumb.

Baker's Note

A large pool of leaked butter suggests underproofing, damaged lamination, or butter that became too warm.

Cut, lengthen, and roll without crushing the layers.

DAY 19

Croissant Diagnosis & Round Two

Yield: About 12

Active time: Varies

Total time: 1–2 days

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind croissant diagnosis & round two through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

Repeat Days 16–18 formula

Step by Step

1. Cut open a croissant from Batch One.

2. Identify the single most important defect.

3. Choose the most likely cause.

4. Repeat the process while deliberately correcting that variable.

5. Photograph both interiors side by side.

What You Should See and Feel

Your second batch should show at least one clear improvement in lamination, proofing, color, or interior structure.

Baker's Note

Butter shattered = too cold. Butter smeared = too warm. Dense crumb = often underproofed or compressed layers.

Use the interior crumb to diagnose lamination and proofing.

DAY 20

Pain au Chocolat

Yield: About 10

Active time: 30 min active

Total time: 3 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind pain au chocolat through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

1 batch laminated croissant dough

Chocolate batons or dark chocolate

Egg wash

Step by Step

1. Roll dough 3–4 mm thick.

2. Cut even rectangles.

3. Place chocolate near one edge, roll once, add a second baton if desired, and finish rolling.

4. Place seam-side down.

5. Proof until expanded.

6. Egg-wash and bake about 18–22 minutes until deeply golden.

What You Should See and Feel

Even rectangles and consistent chocolate placement produce uniform pastries.

Baker's Note

Best fresh; baked pastries can be frozen and gently rewarmed.

DAY 21

Croissants aux Amandes

Yield: 6 almond croissants

Active time: 25 min

Total time: About 1 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind croissants aux amandes through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

6 day-old croissants

100 g (about 1/3 cup + 1 tbsp + 1 tsp) water

100 g (1/2 cup) sugar

100 g (7 tbsp) unsalted butter

100 g (1/2 cup) sugar

100 g (about 1 cup) almond flour

2 eggs

10 g (about 1 tbsp + 1 tsp) all-purpose flour

1 tsp vanilla

Sliced almonds

Confectioners’ sugar

Step by Step

1. Boil water and sugar briefly; cool syrup.

2. Cream butter and sugar; add almond flour, eggs, flour, and vanilla.

3. Slice croissants horizontally.

4. Brush lightly with syrup and spread almond cream inside.

5. Close, spread a little cream on top, and add sliced almonds.

6. Bake at 350°F / 175°C for 15–20 minutes.

7. Cool and dust with confectioners’ sugar.

What You Should See and Feel

The exterior should be crisp and golden while the almond filling remains moist and rich.

Baker's Note

Do not soak croissants heavily in syrup; they should be moistened, not saturated.

Milestone

Photograph your work and write one sentence about the biggest improvement you noticed this week.

DAY 22

Tarte aux Pommes

Yield: 1 9-inch tart

Active time: 35 min

Total time: About 2 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind tarte aux pommes through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

1 pâte sucrée shell

4–5 firm baking apples

30 g (2 tbsp) melted butter

40 g (about 3 tbsp) sugar

Lemon juice

Apricot glaze, optional

Step by Step

1. Peel, core, and slice apples thinly and consistently.

2. Arrange in overlapping concentric circles.

3. Brush lightly with melted butter and sprinkle with sugar.

4. Bake at 375°F / 190°C for roughly 35–50 minutes until apples are tender and pastry fully baked.

5. Brush with a thin apricot glaze if desired.

What You Should See and Feel

Consistent slices create even cooking and a professional pattern.

Baker's Note

Choose apples firm enough to retain shape during baking.

Arrange fruit or apples with deliberate, repeated geometry.

sections.title: DAY 22 COMPLETE ✓
sections.html:
DAY 22 COMPLETE ✓


DAY 23

Profiteroles

Yield: About 18

Active time: 35 min

Total time: About 2 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind profiteroles through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

1 batch pâte à choux

Pastry cream, whipped cream, or ice cream

150 g (about 1 cup chopped) dark chocolate

150 g (about 2/3 cup) heavy cream

Step by Step

1. Prepare and bake choux rounds.

2. Cool completely.

3. Fill with your chosen filling.

4. Heat cream and pour over chocolate; rest and stir smooth.

5. Spoon warm chocolate sauce over profiteroles immediately before serving.

What You Should See and Feel

The shells should remain crisp enough to contrast with the creamy filling.

Baker's Note

Fill close to serving time if you want maximum shell crispness.

sections.title: DAY 23 COMPLETE ✓
sections.html:
DAY 23 COMPLETE ✓


DAY 24

Paris-Brest

Yield: One 8–9 inch pastry

Active time: 50 min

Total time: 3+ hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind paris-brest through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

1 batch pâte à choux

Sliced almonds

Egg wash

500 g pastry cream

100–150 g (about 1/3–1/2 cup) praline paste

150 g (about 2/3 cup) softened butter OR 200 g (about 3/4 cup + 2 tbsp) softly whipped cream

Step by Step

1. Draw an 8-inch circle on parchment and turn it over.

2. Pipe two choux rings side by side and a third over the seam.

3. Egg-wash lightly and scatter sliced almonds.

4. Bake until deeply golden and dry; cool completely.

5. Mix pastry cream with praline paste, then enrich with softened butter or fold with whipped cream.

6. Slice the choux ring horizontally, pipe filling decoratively, replace the top, and dust lightly with confectioners’ sugar.

What You Should See and Feel

The choux ring should be dry enough to hold its shape and the filling should pipe cleanly.

Baker's Note

Do not fill warm choux; heat will soften or melt the cream.

sections.title: DAY 24 COMPLETE ✓
sections.html:
DAY 24 COMPLETE ✓


DAY 25

The Advanced Baguette

Yield: 3 baguettes

Active time: 45 min active

Total time: Overnight + 4 hr

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind the advanced baguette through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

Poolish: 150 g (about 1 1/4 cups) bread flour, 150 g (about 1/2 cup + 2 tbsp) water, tiny pinch instant yeast

Final dough: all poolish, 350 g bread flour, about 190 g water, 10 g (about 1 2/3 tsp) salt, 2 g (about 2/3 tsp) instant yeast

Step by Step

1. Mix poolish the night before and leave until bubbly and aromatic.

2. Combine poolish with flour, most water, and yeast; add salt and adjust with remaining water.

3. Bulk ferment with folds.

4. Divide, preshape, rest, shape, proof, score, steam, and bake as with earlier baguettes.

5. Compare directly with Day 3.

What You Should See and Feel

Look for improved aroma, flavor, scoring, and crumb. The preferment should smell pleasantly fermented, not harsh or rotten.

Baker's Note

Longer controlled fermentation develops flavor; it does not replace proper dough strength and proofing.

sections.title: DAY 25 COMPLETE ✓
sections.html:
DAY 25 COMPLETE ✓


DAY 26

The Croissant Final Exam

Yield: About 12

Active time: Varies

Total time: 1–2 days

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind the croissant final exam through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

Repeat Days 16–18 formula

Step by Step

1. Write the entire croissant process from memory.

2. Prepare dough and butter block.

3. Laminate with controlled temperature and rest periods.

4. Roll, cut, shape, proof, egg-wash, and bake.

5. Score exterior layers, shape, color, flakiness, honeycomb, butter flavor, crispness, and tenderness from 0–5 each.

What You Should See and Feel

Your goal is not perfection; it is a more intentional, better-controlled croissant than Day 18.

Baker's Note

If your score is low, identify the stage—not yourself—that needs more practice.

DAY 27

Build Your French Bakery

Yield: Preparation day

Active time: Varies

Total time: Half day

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind build your french bakery through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

Ingredients for final baguettes, croissants, pain au chocolat, brioche, fruit tart, and éclairs

Step by Step

1. Choose a final serving time and work backward.

2. Prepare long-rest components: croissant dough, butter block, tart dough, pastry cream, brioche dough, and poolish if using it.

3. Write a realistic oven schedule.

4. Group tasks by resting, proofing, baking temperature, cooling, and assembly needs.

What You Should See and Feel

You should see the entire bake as a coordinated system rather than six separate recipes.

Baker's Note

Do not schedule two fragile proofed products to need the oven at the same moment.

DAY 28

The French Bakery Challenge

Photorealistic reference: the complete Day 28 French bakery presentation.

Yield: A complete bakery spread

Active time: Varies

Total time: Full baking session

Today's Mission

Build the core skill behind the french bakery challenge through deliberate practice and observation.

Ingredients

2 baguettes

6 croissants

4 pains au chocolat

1 brioche

1 fruit tart

6 chocolate éclairs

Step by Step

1. Follow your Day 27 production plan.

2. Keep the workspace clean and ingredients organized.

3. Respect dough and butter temperature.

4. Use sensory cues rather than blindly following the clock.

5. Cool and assemble each product appropriately.

6. Arrange the finished spread and photograph it.

7. Compare the photograph with Day 7 and complete your final assessment.

What You Should See and Feel

The final table should show not just variety, but evidence of better shaping, color, organization, and confidence.

Baker's Note

When something goes wrong, diagnose the process. That is what bakers do.

sections.title: Day 28: twenty-eight days of deliberate practice on one table.
sections.html:
Day 28: twenty-eight days of deliberate practice on one table.

Milestone

Photograph your work and write one sentence about the biggest improvement you noticed this week.

DAY 28 COMPLETE ✓


Master Troubleshooting Guide

Bread

Dense crumb: underproofing, weak gluten, weak fermentation, or aggressive shaping.

Pale crust: underbaking, insufficient preheat, or a cool oven.

Gummy interior: underbaking or slicing while hot.

Loaf spreads sideways: weak shaping tension, overproofing, or insufficient dough strength.

Baguettes

Scores do not open: dull blade, poor angle, overproofing, weak surface tension, or insufficient steam.

No ear: scoring may be too perpendicular; use a shallower angle.

Short, thick baguette: allow preshaped dough to relax before final lengthening.

Brioche

Butter will not incorporate: butter too cold or gluten insufficiently developed.

Greasy dough: dough too warm; chill briefly.

Dense brioche: underproofing, weak yeast, or insufficient gluten development.

Tart Dough

Shrinkage: overworking, stretching during lining, warm dough, or insufficient chilling.

Cracks: dough too cold, dry, thin, or roughly handled.

Soggy base: underbaking or overly wet filling.

Pastry Cream

Lumpy: excessive heat or insufficient whisking; sieve while warm.

Too thin: starch may not have cooked sufficiently.

Skin: surface was not covered directly during cooling.

Choux

No rise: batter too loose, panade too wet, or oven too cool.

Collapse: underbaked or interior insufficiently dried.

Batter too runny: prepare a small additional panade and blend it in gradually; do not simply add raw flour.

Croissants

Heavy butter leakage: underproofing, damaged lamination, or excessive warmth.

Butter shatters: butter too cold relative to dough.

Butter smears: butter too warm; refrigerate immediately.

Dense/bread-like interior: underproofing, compressed layers, weak fermentation, or butter incorporated into dough.

Pale exterior: bake longer for rich golden color.

sections.title: Food Safety and Allergen Awareness
sections.html:
Food Safety and Allergen Awareness

Wash hands and clean work surfaces before baking.

Treat flour as a raw ingredient; do not eat raw dough or batter.

Keep raw eggs away from ready-to-eat foods.

Cool and refrigerate pastry cream promptly.

Keep cream-filled pastries refrigerated and do not leave them at room temperature for extended periods.

Common allergens in this book include wheat/gluten, milk, eggs, almonds, hazelnuts and other tree nuts, and possible soy in chocolate products.

Ask guests about allergies and consider cross-contact in shared kitchens.

sections.title: French Baking Glossary
sections.html:
French Baking Glossary

Autolyse

A rest that allows flour to hydrate before further dough development.

Baguette

A long, narrow French loaf.

Banneton

A basket used to support dough during proofing.

Beurrage

Butter prepared for lamination.

Boulanger

A bread baker.

Boulangerie

A bakery specializing primarily in bread and related baked goods.

Boule

A round loaf.

Brioche

A rich yeast dough containing substantial egg and butter.

Couche

A cloth used to support baguettes during proofing.

Crème d'Amande

Almond cream.

Crème Pâtissière

Photorealistic reference: pastry cream from tempering through the finished silky texture.

Pastry cream.

Détrempe

The base dough used in laminated pastry.

Lamination

The process of creating alternating layers of dough and fat.

Mise en Place

Organizing ingredients and tools before beginning.

Pain au Chocolat

Laminated pastry wrapped around chocolate.

Panade

The cooked flour mixture used as the base of pâte à choux.

Pâte à Choux

Cooked pastry dough used for éclairs, profiteroles, and Paris-Brest.

Pâte Sucrée

Sweet tart dough.

Pâtisserie

French pastry; also a pastry shop.

Poolish

A liquid preferment commonly made with equal weights flour and water plus a small amount of yeast.

Proofing

The final rise before baking.

Tour

A turn or fold during lamination.

sections.title: Afterword
sections.html:
Afterword

Day Twenty-Nine

There is something deliberately missing from the title of this book. It does not say Master French Baking Forever in Twenty-Eight Days. No serious craft works that way.

Twenty-eight days gives you something more valuable: a foundation.

Skill develops quietly—one attempt, one observation, one mistake, one correction, one better attempt, then another.

When you began, a recipe may have looked like a list of instructions. Now you can begin asking why: Why is this dough tight? Why did this loaf spread? Why is the butter leaking? Why did the choux collapse? Those questions are evidence of progress.

Tomorrow is Day Twenty-Nine. Choose the recipe that challenged you most and make it again. Sometimes the next level is hidden inside the recipe you already know.

Bienvenue à la boulangerie. Welcome to the bakery—and welcome to your next batch.

KDP Publishing Metadata

Book Description

What if you could go from complete beginner to confidently baking baguettes, croissants, brioche, éclairs, fruit tarts, and other French classics in four focused weeks?

French Baking in 28 Days is a step-by-step training program designed to teach how French baking works. Beginning with your first simple dough, each day builds on the techniques before it, progressing through baguettes, brioche, pâte sucrée, pastry cream, choux, éclairs, croissants, pain au chocolat, almond croissants, Paris-Brest, and a complete French bakery challenge.

Every stage includes metric measurements, visual and tactile cues, troubleshooting guidance, and deliberate repetition. You do not need culinary-school experience. You need basic measuring tools, patience, and twenty-eight days; a kitchen scale is helpful but not required.
